## 374544: an exact witness, then the whole published mechanism

Literal endpoint: for every positive k and n_i, R(n_1 P3,...,n_k P3) equals 2 max n_i + sum n_i - k + 1. A single in-scope colouring disproves this universal equality.

Take k=3 and n_1=n_2=n_3=1. On vertices a,b,c,d give ab and cd colour 1, ac and bd colour 2, ad and bc colour 3. These are all six edges, each exactly once. Every colour class is a matching, so no vertex has two incident edges of one colour, which is necessary for a monochromatic three-vertex path. Thus this colouring of K4 contains no requested P3. The asserted formula gives 3, whereas R(P3,P3,P3)>4. Conversely at a vertex of K5, four incident edges have only three colours, so two have the same colour, yielding a P3 on three distinct vertices. Therefore the exact value is 5.

This was not stopped at a small witness. Source arXiv:2605.02793v1, Theorem 1.2 and Lemma 2.2 with its proof, already gives R >= 2 ceil(k/2)+sum n_i-k+1. Its construction starts with a factorization of K_(2 ceil(k/2)) into matchings and then adjoins n_i-1 vertices in successive colour-i blocks. Every colour-i P3 uses at least one vertex in its own block: outside that block, earlier edges of that colour form only a matching and later vertices have no colour-i incident edges. Consequently n_i vertex-disjoint P3s cannot exist. The K4 witness is precisely the k=3, all-one instance; no unpaid witness family remains.

The source's Theorem 1.9 and Section 3 instead prove the formula for Gallai colourings, which exclude rainbow triangles. Our K4 contains a rainbow triangle. The source's later Lemma 2.13 also supplies a different obstruction: two colour-1 K5s and five cross perfect matchings on K10 avoid three colour-1 cherries and any cherry in the other five colours. This further confirms that the missing Gallai restriction is mathematical, not typographical notation. No claim is made that the all-colourings formula is an unresolved conjecture in the source.

Gates: exact literal negation proved; source refutation already public May 4, 2026; routine source instance and scope correction, novelty/significance fail. No Pi plan.

## 373490: pursue the equality case, then identify the exact public proof

Literal endpoint is uniqueness, not just the Fibonacci upper bound. Definitions from arXiv:2603.07296v1 Section 2 matter: 'simple assembly' means a connected rigid graph admitting a transverse Euler trail; loops and parallel edges are permitted. Polygonal paths visit distinct rigid vertices and turn between adjacent half-edges. Singletons count; cycles do not. Hamiltonian means a vertex-disjoint family covering every rigid vertex. Graph isomorphisms preserve cyclic half-edge orders. Replacing this with an ordinary simple graph would not be faithful.

Here is the complete reduction to the published word theorem, with the nontrivial source inputs separated. Read Proposition 3.5, Proposition 3.6 and its four implications, Corollary 3.10, Lemmas 4.1 and 4.6, Theorem 4.7 and Corollary 4.8. The Cambridge journal body has the same numbered endpoint, published March 5, 2026, before the March 7 arXiv posting.

Follow the transverse trail and write its rigid vertices as a double occurrence word w of length 2n. Number its internal edges 1,...,2n-1. A Hamiltonian path set determines its selected edge positions. They cannot be consecutive, since consecutive trail edges go straight through a rigid vertex, rather than turning; separate paths cannot share that vertex. Selected edges and the unused singleton vertices determine the path set uniquely. The alternating selection 1,3,...,2n-1 has n edges and cannot be a path forest on n vertices. Binary strings of length m with no adjacent ones are counted by b_m=b_(m-1)+b_(m-2), b_0=1,b_1=2, hence b_m=F_(m+2). This yields the bound F_(2n+1)-1.

Equality forces every other nonconsecutive edge selection to be a polygonal path forest. It is equivalent to saying that after deleting any nonempty proper set of letters from w, some remaining maximal contiguous block has odd length. To check this bridge: if every block has even length, pair consecutive positions in each block. These give at most n-1 pairwise nonconsecutive trail edges, and every remaining vertex occurs twice as an endpoint. A finite graph of degree two at every used vertex contains a cycle, violating the forest requirement. Conversely if a nonconsecutive selection contains a cycle, keep exactly its vertex letters; each kept occurrence must pair with its neighbour along a selected edge. The remaining contiguous blocks therefore have even lengths. Nonconsecutivity ensures at most two selected half-edges per vertex and, when there are two, they turn. This also covers loops and double edges as cycles.

The parity property rules out a concatenation of two nonempty double occurrence words: delete all letters of one, leaving the other of even length. Lemma 4.1 then produces a framing tangled-cord subsequence. Its construction begins with the first letter and repeatedly chooses a crossing letter with farthest second occurrence. Failure to reach the last position would give a closed prefix and a decomposition. The farthest-occurrence choice prevents an extension from reaching back past an earlier cord stage, so the selected letters have the tangled-cord order.

Lemma 4.6 supplies the decisive second step, beyond mere framing. For an even-length word with a framing cord of s letters and extra positions, some nonempty subset of cord letters can be removed leaving only even blocks. Induct on s. If an intermediate second occurrence is even, cut at it and apply induction to the shorter framing prefix; the omitted suffix has even length and the removed letters have no occurrences there. The prefix is strictly longer than its cord because the next cord letter first appears inside it. If an intermediate first occurrence is odd, reverse the whole even-length word to obtain the preceding case. Otherwise all interior first occurrences are even and all interior second occurrences odd. Delete all framing letters. Consecutive framing occurrences then have opposite position parity, including the first and last boundary pairs, so every intervening block has even length. The base s=1 removes the two end occurrences. Since extra positions exist, this is a proper subset of all word letters. Thus extra letters contradict equality's parity property.

The framing cord must consequently use every letter: w is exactly the tangled-cord word up to renaming and reversal. The converse, attainment by that word, is the source's Theorem 3.1 discussion citing Burns et al. (2013), Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.4; no independent reconstruction of the entire 2013 counting proof is claimed. Equivalently one may apply the exact if-and-only-if Corollary 4.8 directly: its variables, Hamiltonian counting convention and isomorphism notion match the literal record. This is a complete source-dependent proof of the requested statement, not an independent new proof of all source dependencies.

## 368260: uniform width route sustained, still missing mathematics

The meaningful endpoint is a single constant C valid for all nonperfect (claw,4K1,bridge)-free graphs. Read arXiv:2505.00202v1, Theorems 1.2, 5.10, 6.23, 7.17; clique-width definitions, Lemma 2.7 and its partner-path construction; Section 9 Conjecture 9.1. 'Bridge' is the specific induced forbidden graph of Figure 1, not an edge whose deletion disconnects a graph. Its printed six-vertex diagram was located, but its exact adjacency was not independently transcribed. This is an explicit semantic gap for any finite witness.

First shortcut fails: each finite graph has finite clique-width, so bounding width by |V(G)| proves only a vacuous per-graph reading. It does not establish the uniform class assertion intended by the source. No credit for that quantifier correction.

Second route partitions vertices by their neighbourhood on an induced C5 (at most 32 types), and tries to replace each type by a module or a bounded number of cliques. Finite type count alone does not control internal edges or adjacency between types: an arbitrary two-clique graph has only two clique classes yet can carry an arbitrary bipartite adjacency matrix between them. A source lemma is needed to force modules or restricted cross-neighbourhoods. The source proves such restrictions in the stronger class with the C4-twin forbidden. They cannot simply be transferred to this reservation.

Third route uses the actual source row-labelling lemma. If t clique parts have only matching or co-matching relations around a cycle and all other pairs are joins or co-joins, build a partner graph of degree at most two. Its components are paths and cycles. Processing one component at a time with old/new labels per part, plus a temporary label, gives at most 2t+1 labels. This explains why the published proof can give a uniform bound without bounding graph order. Missing lemma: in the C5/C6 case without the C4-twin restriction, obtain a bounded number of such clique parts or an alternative bounded-rank-width decomposition. The source expressly identifies twelve uses of the removed restriction; no replacement proof was found.

A fourth check prevents a false reduction via the strong perfect graph theorem. 4K1 excludes holes of length >=8; it does not exclude all large odd antiholes, whose independence number is two. The source also uses the C4-twin restriction to exclude antiholes. Any proof covering only C5 and C7 cases must supply a new antihole argument after dropping that restriction. The published C7 case alone is not the exact full endpoint.

The thesis 'Properties of (claw, 4K1, bridge)-free graphs' (LaGrange, 2023) is a material companion. Its public landing page was read; it describes the C7 case and stronger-class result. ## 363618: endpoint correction and a second genuine route

Source arXiv:2406.14153v1 Definition 5.1 defines fall-off on the symmetric slice t in [0,1/2], with joint-event correlation body L and pairwise-consistency relaxation N. Conjecture 10.6 is the treewidth formula. Read Propositions 8.9, 10.5/10.7 discussion and the concluding scope.

A literal edgeless example is already an excluded domain correction: for K1 there are no pair coordinates, both sliced bodies are the same zero-dimensional point, their volumes agree, and fall-off is the capped endpoint 1/2, whereas tw(K1)=0 gives 1. This says nothing new about the intended nontrivial graph family. No credit.

Beyond that shortcut, attempt a tree-decomposition proof by gluing bag distributions. Bag size <=w+1 suggests the scale 1/(w+1), but edge marginals alone do not give mutually consistent full distributions on overlapping separators. Proving a bag-distribution extension theorem at exactly that scale is the missing lower-bound bridge. Separately, equality needs an obstruction active at that scale in every width-w graph; a treewidth-w graph need not contain a (w+1)-clique. Replacing treewidth by clique number would lose the cyclic examples.

A facet route is more exact. For each fixed normalized pair vector x, put p_i=t and q_ij=t*x_ij. In the cone of nonnegative nonempty assignment weights, let weights a_S satisfy sum_(S containing i) a_S=1 and sum_(S containing i,j) a_S=x_ij. A probability distribution at scale t exists precisely when some such weights have total <=1/t, filling unused mass at the empty assignment. Thus the minimum total assignment mass controls where an individual ray exits the joint correlation body. This is an elementary rescaling equivalence, not a solution of the volume-ratio problem. To turn it into fall-off requires control of the whole feasible normalized region, its boundary facets, and positive-volume changes. Source Proposition 10.7 only excludes inclusion-exclusion facets as counterexamples; it does not classify all facets. No complete nontrivial witness or all-graph equality proof was obtained.
